title: Concept Drills — Heredity And Evolution (Class 12 Biology)
subject: biology

questions.question: A student hears 'the allele for six fingers (polydactyly) is dominant' and concludes most humans must have six fingers. What is the flaw?
questions.solution: Dominant describes what happens IN a heterozygote (the allele expresses itself), not how COMMON the allele is in the population. Allele frequency is set by mutation, selection and drift — most dominant disease alleles are rare because selection removes them. Polydactyly is dominant yet rare (~1 in 500); the recessive five-finger allele is near-universal. 'Dominant' wins the genotype battle; it says nothing about winning the population.

questions.question: Two genes on the SAME chromosome, very close together, are crossed in a dihybrid. A student still predicts 9:3:3:1. Why will the actual ratio deviate, and toward what?
questions.solution: 9:3:3:1 assumes independent assortment — alleles of the two genes shuffle freely into gametes. Linked genes on one chromosome travel TOGETHER, so parental gamete combinations are over-produced and recombinant ones are rare (only via crossing over). The F2 ratio collapses toward 3:1-like parental classes with few recombinants. Mendel was lucky: his seven pea genes sit on different chromosomes (or far apart). Linkage is exactly why Morgan's fruit-fly crosses 'broke' Mendel's ratio.

questions.question: DNA polymerase 'reads 3′→5′ and builds 5′→3′.' A student asks why the lagging strand can't just be built 3′→5′ continuously like the leading strand. What forbids it?
questions.solution: Chemistry forbids it: DNA polymerase can only ADD a nucleotide's 5′-phosphate to a free 3′-OH end — the enzyme's active site works in one direction only. On the lagging strand the template runs 5′→3′ toward the fork, so continuous 5′→3′ synthesis would have to move AWAY from the fork (backwards). The cell's workaround is Okazaki fragments: short 5′→3′ stretches built away-from-fork, later stitched by ligase. One enzyme direction → two strand strategies.

questions.question: A harmful recessive allele (e.g. cystic fibrosis) persists for generations despite killing homozygotes young. Why can't selection eliminate it, and what hides it?
questions.solution: Selection sees PHENOTYPES, not genotypes — and the allele hides in healthy heterozygote carriers (Aa), who survive and reproduce normally. Only the rare aa homozygotes ($q^2$ of the population) are removed each generation, while the vast reservoir $2pq$ of carrier copies passes on untouched. The rarer the allele, the larger the hidden fraction: at $q = 0.02$, carriers outnumber sufferers ~100 to 1. Recessive lethals are nearly invisible to selection — that is why they linger. (Heterozygote advantage, as in sickle-cell vs malaria, can actively preserve them.)
